prompt: Put the shares of Apple's phased release in the order of its seven days.
On day 2 of the planner's phased release, a student opens the App Store and taps Update. What do they get?

choices.text: The old version, because she is outside the 2%
choices.why: Phasing applies only to automatic updates.

choices.text: Nothing until day 7
choices.why: Manual downloads are never held back.

choices.text: The new version
choices.why: Right. Anybody can download it by hand at any time.

choices.text: A message to join a waiting list
choices.why: There is no such list.

prompt: For how many days in total can an App Store phased release be paused?
What can Google Play's staged rollout do that Apple's phased release cannot?

choices.text: Choose the percentages and days
choices.why: Right. Apple's seven steps are fixed.

choices.text: Release to everybody at once
choices.why: Apple can too, at any point.

choices.text: Stop the release reaching new people
choices.why: Apple can pause, which does that.

choices.text: Take the release back from phones
choices.why: Neither store can do that.

prompt: 1.5.0 is crashing. The team says "roll back to 1.4.0". What can it actually publish?

choices.text: The 1.4.0 build again, with its old version code
choices.why: A lower, used code is refused.

choices.text: Nothing until the next planned release
choices.why: A roll-forward can be released whenever it is ready.

choices.text: A request to the store to restore 1.4.0
choices.why: Neither store offers that.

choices.text: A 1.5.1 with 1.4.0's code and a higher version code
choices.why: Right. Rolling forward is the only way back.

prompt: 1.5.0 migrated the planner's database to a new schema. Why would installing 1.4.0 on top be dangerous even if a store allowed it?

choices.text: 1.4.0 would be signed with a different key
choices.why: Same key; the problem is the data.

choices.text: It would open a database it does not understand
choices.why: Right. The data has moved on.

choices.text: The store listing would show the wrong version
choices.why: The listing is not what breaks.

choices.text: The phone would refuse an older Android API level
choices.why: API level is not the issue here.

prompt: Match what a team says during an incident to what it can actually do.

pairs.right: release a higher version with the old code
halt the rollout; installed copies stay
flip a remote switch built in before release

right_distractors: delete the version from every phone

prompt: Why does `rollout.ts` use a hash of the install for the bucket, rather than a random number each day?

choices.text: Random numbers are too slow in Node
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: To keep the same people in
choices.why: Right. Day 3's group contains day 2's, as the rollout grows.

choices.text: Hashes give more crashes
choices.why: The hash decides who, not how many.

choices.text: Google requires FNV-1a
choices.why: Google picks users its own way.

prompt: On day 1, 1.5.0 was 1.5 points below 1.4.0. Why did the rule not halt then?

choices.text: The drop was below half a point
choices.why: It was 1.5 points, above the limit.

choices.text: Apple's schedule forbids halting on day 1
choices.why: Pausing is allowed any day.

choices.text: 1.4.0 was also crashing
choices.why: Its rate was the baseline, 99.46%.

choices.text: 195 people were too few for the rate to mean much
choices.why: Right. Below 500, a handful of crashes moves the rate by a point.

prompt: In the simulation, by how many percentage points did 1.5.0's crash-free rate trail 1.4.0's on day 3? Answer to two decimals.
Where does a real rollout get the crash numbers the simulation invents?

choices.text: The crash reporter and the consoles
choices.why: Right. Lesson 12 and Android vitals.

choices.text: From the testers' feedback
choices.why: Production is past the testers.

choices.text: From the server's error log, which sees every request
choices.why: A crash on the phone often never reaches the server.

choices.text: From the store reviews people leave about the update
choices.why: Reviews are words, late and few.

prompt: After the halt on day 3, what happens to the 1011 installs on 1.5.0?

choices.text: The store replaces it with 1.4.0 overnight
choices.why: No store reaches into a phone like that.

choices.text: The app stops opening until they reinstall
choices.why: A halt does not disable anything.

choices.text: They keep it until an update reaches them
choices.why: Right. The halt protects only the people who did not have it yet.

choices.text: They are moved back to 1.4.0 when they next open the app
choices.why: Nothing moves a phone back.

prompt: Put the incident's moves in the lesson's order.
items: halt the rollout, pause the phased release
find the cause in the crash reports
build 1.5.1 with a higher version code
release 1.5.1 fast, first to the people on 1.5.0

prompt: Which of these could have turned 1.5.0's broken feature off within minutes on the phones that had it?

choices.text: A remote switch shipped before 1.5.0
choices.why: Right. Read at start-up, it has to be in the version that is broken.

choices.text: An expedited review
choices.why: It speeds the fix, not the phones already broken.

choices.text: A forced-update screen added in 1.5.1
choices.why: It would be in 1.5.1, which those phones do not have.

choices.text: Halting the rollout sooner
choices.why: It would protect others, not the ones who have it.

prompt: A team argues that a one-line copy change does not need a staged rollout. What does the lesson's last section answer?

choices.text: Agreed, small changes can go to 100%
choices.why: The bug in 1.5.0 was in a change called trivial.

choices.text: Copy changes do not need review either
choices.why: Everything is reviewed.

choices.text: Stage every production release
choices.why: Right. Small is a guess; staging is a rule.

choices.text: It depends on the store
choices.why: The rule is the same in both.

prompt: Which of these does a halted Google Play rollout do? Choose every one.

choices.text: Stop the release reaching new people
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Remove the release from phones that have it
choices.why: Installed copies stay.

choices.text: Keep the users already picked, if it is resumed
choices.why: Right. Picked users stay picked.

choices.text: Restore the previous version for everybody
choices.why: There is no rollback.

prompt: A React Native team wants its Android and iOS halves at the same share each day. What does it have to do?

choices.text: Nothing; Expo syncs the two stores
choices.why: The stores are separate, and nothing syncs them.

choices.text: Move Google's percentages by hand on Apple's schedule
choices.why: Right. Apple's ramp moves daily; Google's moves when you move it.

choices.text: Use the same version code on both
choices.why: Codes do not set percentages.

choices.text: Release iOS only after Android reaches 100%
choices.why: That is the opposite of the same share each day.
